definition: Two named debris techniques look alike (both render explosion/impact debris as simple cube shapes) but differ in exactly one dimension the source states directly: 'cubic debris' (on-screen label) is purely decorative — cubes fly around with no particular sense of timing, chosen because cubes are easy to draw from any perspective — while 'Yutapon cubes' (on-screen label, credited to animator Yutaka Nakamura) are timing-DEPENDENT, built around a deliberate hold-then-release beat rather than continuous scatter.
purpose: Choose deliberately between a purely decorative debris shape and a timing-carrying one, rather than treating 'cube-shaped debris' as a single undifferentiated look.
visible_effect: Cubic debris: small dark cube shapes scattered continuously across an impact/explosion with no held pause (confirmed in this session's frame at t=01:58, cubes strewn across a cracked white surface). Yutapon cubes: a cluster of pale cube/particle shapes that holds in place around a moving subject before releasing outward on a timed beat (confirmed in this session's frame at t=02:15, cube particles trailing a diving figure against water).
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: Cubic debris reads as generic environmental destruction dressing; Yutapon cubes' hold-then-release specifically emphasizes the INSTANT of release as a beat, the same emphasis-through-timing mechanism this batch's other impact/beat techniques rely on.
physical_interpretation: Neither is physically realistic — the source notes cubic debris is 'a more unrealistic way of drawing debris' chosen because cubes are easy to draw consistently across perspectives, not because real debris is cuboid.
use_cases: cubic debris: continuous environmental destruction dressing (explosions, wreckage) where no specific beat needs marking
Yutapon cubes: a charge-up-and-release beat (a power attack, an energy build) where the audience should feel one specific instant of release, not a continuous scatter
non_use_cases: using continuous, untimed cubic debris where the audience needs a clear held-then-released beat — the source is explicit that ordinary cubic debris 'flies around everywhere without any sense of timing', which would blur exactly the beat Yutapon cubes exist to mark
using the timed hold-and-release Yutapon-cube structure for background destruction dressing that doesn't need a beat, adding unnecessary held-frame cost
interactions: layered_anticipation, readable_hold_duration (LESSONS.md check #4), weight_strength_beat_sequence (W02, v19) — Yutapon cubes' hold-then-release is another named instance of this batch's recurring hold-before-release timing family, applied to a particle/debris layer rather than to the character's own pose

external_force_easing_mismatch (LESSONS.md check #10, next to be built) — the same marker-plus-motion-curve data that check would use (a declared event marker crossed against a motion curve) is exactly what would distinguish a genuine held-then-released beat from continuous scatter
pose_hold_density (W01, v1) — the general hold-duration vocabulary that Yutapon cubes' particle-layer hold is a specific application of

style_variations.anime: both are native anime VFX vocabulary per the source; cubic debris is described as popularized among 'web-gen' (digitally-native) animators generally, Yutapon cubes specifically by Yutaka Nakamura and animators he inspired
style_variations.realistic: neither applies — both are explicit non-physical stylizations of debris

cadence_representation: The cube SHAPE itself is a VFX-authoring detail Cadence could reach today (a particle emitter with a cube mesh/texture, no different in kind from any other emitter shape `ai/vfxspec.js` already supports); the more valuable half — the timing-dependent hold-then-release distinction — is not represented as a named pattern, but is built from data this build already has: a declared event marker (`ai/events.js`) plus the emitter/particle system's own timeline.
control_surface: `vfx_new_effect`/`vfx_add_layer` can already author a cube-shaped emitter; no named preset currently distinguishes a 'hold then release' timing profile from continuous emission.
detection_and_measurement_methods: The shape choice itself is not motion data and is not measurable; the TIMING distinction is: a near-zero-velocity hold phase on the emitter/attachment immediately followed by a sharp velocity spike at a declared marker is checkable with `ai/motion.js sampleMotion` against `ai/events.js` markers, the same measurement shape as check #4 (`readable_hold_duration`) and check #27 (`weight_strength_beat_sequence`).
generation_or_modification_methods: A cube-shaped particle emitter is authorable today via `vfx_add_layer`; a named 'charge-hold-release' emission preset does not exist.
failure_modes: treating the two as interchangeable because they look similar in a single still frame, losing the timing distinction that is the source's whole point
applying Yutapon-style held timing to background dressing with no beat to mark, wasting a held frame's worth of anticipation on something the audience isn't meant to track
applying continuous cubic-debris scatter to a moment meant to read as a single charged release, diluting the beat
roblox_considerations: A `ParticleEmitter` with a cube-shaped texture/mesh reaches the visual shape directly; the hold-then-release timing would be authored as an emission-rate or `Enabled` toggle keyed to the same marker driving the character's own charge/release pose, not a property of the particle system alone.
performance_implications: A held cluster of particles (Yutapon cubes) that then bursts is likely a brief spike in active-particle count at the release instant rather than a sustained cost, opposite to continuous cubic-debris scatter's steadier ongoing cost; inferred, not stated by the source.
examples: 'cubic debris is the name says it when debris are cubes... it's a stylistic choice for visual pleasurement... a good example is Hiro Mashima [creator name as heard] that uses cubic debris quite a bit' (video @ 01:53–02:21), confirmed on-screen label 'cubic debris' in this session's frames at t=01:58

'Yutapon cubes are more timing dependent, there's a big emphasis on the hold and release, where for cubic debris it just flies around everywhere without any sense of timing... popularized by Yutaka Nakamura' (video @ 02:32–02:47), confirmed on-screen label 'yutapon cubes' in this session's frames at t=02:15/02:48, credited on-screen to 'Shingo Yamashita, Key Animation' for the specific cut shown
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/iMV9Tlpo1wY (SinChi) @ 01:53–03:05 — the presenter states the definitional distinction directly and both names are confirmed by on-screen corner labels ('cubic debris', 'yutapon cubes') rather than relying on the auto-caption transcript alone, which mistranscribed the latter as 'uton cubes'; experimental until validated
